name: Ab Wheel Rollout
tierNote: Safety tier A (content.md appendix B); census.json difficulty tier 1.

claims.text: Kneel on a soft pad with the hands on the ab wheel, about shoulder-width apart, the wheel on the floor just in front of the knees.

quotes.text: Sit with your knees on a soft pad, and place the ab wheel on the floor in front of you.
quotes.where: How to Do Kneeling Ab Wheel Roll-Outs, step 1

quotes.text: Start by kneeling on the floor with your hands on the ab wheel, placed directly in front of your knees.
quotes.where: How to Perform Ab Wheel Rollouts

quotes.text: Kneel and grip a wheel or barbell, loaded with round plates, with your hands set shoulder-width apart.
quotes.where: 1. Ab Rollout, How To Do It

claims.text: Brace the core and slowly roll the wheel forward until the body is a straight line from knees to head, keeping the back straight the whole time.

quotes.text: Engage your core and slowly roll the wheel forward until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your head.
quotes.where: How to Perform Ab Wheel Rollouts

quotes.text: Be sure to keep your back straight and your core engaged throughout the entire movement.
quotes.where: How to Perform Ab Wheel Rollouts

quotes.text: Roll out as far as you can, and maintain a straight back throughout the movement.
quotes.where: How to Do Kneeling Ab Wheel Roll-Outs, step 2

claims.text: As the arms reach forward overhead and the chest sinks toward the floor, do not let the low back arch.

quotes.text: Extend your hips toward the floor and let your chest sink forward toward the ground. Avoid arching your lower back as you extend your arms above your head.
quotes.where: 1. Ab Rollout, How To Do It

claims.text: Roll the wheel back toward the knees with control, pulling with the lats, to the start.

quotes.text: Reverse the movement with control, and return to the starting position.
quotes.where: How to Do Kneeling Ab Wheel Roll-Outs, step 3

quotes.text: Squeeze your lat muscles and pull yourself back to the starting position.
quotes.where: 1. Ab Rollout, How To Do It

claims.text: Move slowly: rolling out too fast and rushing can increase the risk of the torso rotating or extending. Every rep, squeeze the glutes and start the movement with the core, not by starting the roll with the arms.

quotes.text: Tempo is important. Rolling out too fast and rushing through this movement can increase your risk of torso rotation/extension.
Every rep cue yourself to squeeze the glutes and initiate the movement with the core, as opposed to starting the roll with the arms.

claims.text: The rollout carries an inherent risk of injury and, without proper progressions, can injure the low back. One coach's readiness test: a one-minute plank with about 5-11 kg (10-25 lb), or an easy one-minute hollow-body hold.

quotes.text: The ab rollout is a slightly tougher core exercise, and without proper progressions can actually increase injury to areas like the lower back.
quotes.where: The Benefits of Ab Rollouts and Progressions to Perform Them (intro)

quotes.text: This is an exercise that comes with an inherent risk of injury, so they shouldn’t be performed haphazardly in a program.

If you can hold a weighted plank with (10-25 lbs) for a minute, then there’s a good chance you can experiment with ab rollouts safely. Second, if you can perform a hollow body hold for a minute with ease.
quotes.where: Should You Use the Ab Rollout?

claims.text: Progress by range: start with a short roll-out and go further as you get stronger; rolling against a wall sets a fixed stop, moved further away over time. Kneeling is the easier version; rolling out from the feet is much harder and suits experienced lifters.

quotes.text: try moving through a limited set range of motion before working to your full extension on the ab wheel.
The farther forward you roll out from your body, the harder the move will be. So shorten your range of motion if need be.
you can limit your range of motion by performing kneeling ab-wheels facing a wall. Have the wall stop you at a suitable distance, and then work on increasing your distance to the wall over time.
The exercise is easier when done on your knees, and harder when on your feet.
It’s suitable for experienced fitness enthusiasts looking for an even greater challenge.

claims.text: A case report describes two spinal cord injuries from a fall while using an abdominal roller; both happened during the standing rollout by a patient who was drunk, and the report warns that using ab rollers may result in extremely serious disabilities.

quotes.text: Spinal cord injury without radiological abnormality due to a fall while using an abdominal roller: A report of two cases.
Two cases of spinal cord injuries caused by a roller are reported.
In both cases, injuries occurred during the standing rollout by a patient in an inebriated state
Because the use of abdominal rollers may result in extremely serious disabilities, it is necessary to emphasize the appropriate use of such equipment.

claims.text: The abs are the target: the rectus abdominis holds the body straight, the obliques keep the upper body stable, and the lats also work.

quotes.text: Primary muscles worked: Abs Secondary muscles worked: Obliques
quotes.where: Muscles Worked in Kneeling Ab Wheel Roll-Outs

quotes.text: Your rectus abdominis gets a thorough thrashing as it works overtime to keep your entire body straight as you roll out and to bring you back to the starting position.
The internal and external oblique muscles are fully engaged to keep your upper body stable during the movement.
Muscles Worked Abdominals, lats

claims.text: In an EMG study of 21 adults, the roll-out on a wheel device (the Power Wheel) was among the exercises with the highest upper and lower abdominal, internal oblique and lat activity, while low-back muscle activity was low; applied to the ab wheel by similarity.

quotes.text: Upper and lower rectus abdominis, internal oblique, and latissimus dorsi muscle EMG activity were highest for the Power Wheel (pike, knee-up, and roll-out), hanging knee-up with straps, and reverse crunch inclined 30 degrees.
Lumbar paraspinal muscle EMG activity was low and similar among exercises.
Twenty-one men and women who were healthy and between 23 and 43 years of age were recruited for this study.
Sets & Reps 2-4 x 5-10

claims.text: The rollout needs coordination and self-awareness to avoid injury: the torso nearing lumbar extension or torso rotation can result in injury, and the lighter ab wheel needs more core control to avoid rotation and extension.

quotes.text: This is a movement that requires coordination an self awareness to avoid injury, and can be useful method for teaching athletes to monitor their torso positioning when nearing times like lumbar extension or torso rotation, which can result in injury.
quotes.where: The Benefits of Ab Rollouts and Progressions to Perform Them (intro, Coordination & Awareness)

quotes.text: In addition, they’re lighter in weight, so they require more core control to avoid rotation and extension.

claims.text: Tempo: the roll-out is slow and the return is controlled; no rollout source gives seconds for either phase, so the plate's 2 s down (the roll-out) and 1 s up (the roll back) is a drawing convention.

quotes.text: Engage your core and slowly roll the wheel forward until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your head.
quotes.where: How to Perform Ab Wheel Rollouts

quotes.text: Reverse the movement with control, and return to the starting position.
quotes.where: How to Do Kneeling Ab Wheel Roll-Outs, step 3

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the knees-to-head line (c2), the low-back arch fault (c3) and the roll distance (c7) read from the side.
plate.equipment: Ab wheel composed (census 'abWheel', compose): a small wheel with a handle each side; a soft pad under the knees (c1); floor line.
plate.start: Kneeling on the pad, hands on the wheel handles about shoulder-width, wheel on the floor just in front of the knees (c1); core braced (c2).
plate.end: Rolled out: arms reaching forward overhead, chest low toward the floor, body a straight line from knees to head, low back not arched (c2, c3). Drawn at a moderate roll-out, the kneeling version (c7).

checkpoints.label: Straight line
checkpoints.what: Knees to head in one line; back straight.

checkpoints.label: No back arch
checkpoints.what: Low back doesn't arch as you reach.

checkpoints.label: Roll slowly
checkpoints.what: Slow and controlled, out and back.

mistake.what: Low back arching as the arms reach forward overhead.
mistake.why: BarBend ties lumbar extension (the low back arching) to injury (c13) and says to avoid arching the lower back as the arms extend overhead (c3); rolling out too fast can increase the risk of extension (c5). LR-31 step 2, with step 3's count deciding the tie with torso rotation (rankNote).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: the low back arching (lumbar extension) (c13, c3). Step 1 finds no frequency word for a fault of this exercise. Set aside: BarBend's "it’s not something most can easily pick up and start doing right away" is about who can do the exercise, not a fault; its "Typically, ab wheels will be much smaller and lower to the ground compared to the above two progressions" ('Ab Wheel Rollout') is about the equipment, not a fault; StrengthLog's "The first is accessible for most people, while the second is one of the most demanding core exercises you can do." is about who can do the kneeling version, not a fault; and its "many ab exercises (and exercises for other muscle groups) benefit from performing the movements relatively slowly" sits in its dead bug section and is about exercises in general (R-LB7-3); BarBend's "Most stomach movements, such as crunches and knee raises, flex the abs." is about other exercises. No read source has a common-mistakes list for the rollout. Step 2: BarBend's "This is a movement that requires coordination an self awareness to avoid injury, and can be useful method for teaching athletes to monitor their torso positioning when nearing times like lumbar extension or torso rotation, which can result in injury." (c13) ties two named faults to harm, the low back arching and the torso rotating. Tie: neither is on a common-mistakes list; one source each ties it to harm; both are sourced directly; that sentence names lumbar extension first, but the same page also names them the other way ("torso rotation/extension", c5), so step 3's count is given too (D-SUP-LB6-CCP), the read sources that tell the lifter to avoid each (sources, not lists): low back arching 2 (BarBend best-ab "Avoid arching your lower back as you extend your arms above your head.", c3; BarBend ab-rollouts "they require more core control to avoid rotation and extension", c13); torso rotation 1 (BarBend ab-rollouts, c13). Not counted, as they only give the right position: StrengthLog's "Be sure to keep your back straight" and "maintain a straight back throughout the movement" (c2). The arch leads 2 to 1, so no list tie-break is needed. Set aside at step 2: rolling out too fast (c5, "Rolling out too fast and rushing through this movement can increase your risk of torso rotation/extension.") is a speed fault tied to the two faults, not to harm, and is never drawable; "without proper progressions can actually increase injury to areas like the lower back" and "This is an exercise that comes with an inherent risk of injury" (c6) and the case report's standing rollout falls (c8) are progression or version choices, not candidates; StrengthLog's "You should feel a stretch but not pain." is in its Jefferson curl steps, another exercise, and its "you should be careful not to do too much too soon, as that increases your risk of injury" is about weekly sets. Also set aside, from the fetcher's scan: BarBend's "After all, the last thing you want to do is injure yourself performing an additional accessory movement." and 'Wrapping Up' "as it does come with an inherent risk of injury" are about the exercise as a whole, with no fault named (the same reason as c6's "inherent risk of injury"; c6's "without proper progressions can actually increase injury to areas like the lower back" ties harm to skipping progressions, a programming choice, not a position or movement during the set); the case report's "there are few reports of such injuries caused by a roller" is about how often injuries are reported, names no fault, and 'few' is not a step-1 word; StrengthLog's 'Benefits of Strong Abs' lines ("A solid core makes you less likely to suffer from lower back pain.") are benefits, and its lying leg raise and dead bug lines are other exercises; BarBend's 'Boost Spinal Stability' lines ("to prevent the athlete from experiencing a severe injury like a slipped disc or muscle tear") are about loaded lifts; Escamilla's rectus femoris line ("may be problematic for some people with low back problems") is about the pike, knee-up and other exercises, not the roll-out, and names no fault. drawable stays true: the side view shows the low back arched as the arms reach overhead, a still sign. Pick unchanged; handlingMistakes[0] is already the arch.

tells.text: Back stays straight all the way

tempo.text: Drawing convention (WEAK c14): 'down' is the roll-out, slow ("slowly roll the wheel forward", c14, c2); 'up' is the roll back, with control (c14, c4); no source gives seconds, so 2 s down and 1 s up only show a slower roll-out than return (R-LB7-6). Pause 0: no quote on the card asks for a pause right after the roll back (LR-33). BarBend's 'Make It Harder: Pause at the bottom of each repetition to build strength while your abs are stretched.' (not cited on the card) is a pause at full roll-out, a harder option with no seconds; it is not the pause field.

plate.variantLine: Kneeling version drawn (c1, c7). The standing roll-out is the hard version for experienced lifters (c7) and the one in the fall cases (c8).

grip.type: Both hands on the ab wheel's handles (c1).
grip.note: No rollout source gives the thumb, wrist or how the handle sits in the hand; listed in gaps for the push archetype check (LIB-12 hand pair).

setup.step: Hands on the wheel, about shoulder-width.
Wheel on the floor just in front of your knees.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
New to it? Roll toward a wall that stops you.

posture.point: Knees to head in one straight line.
Start with your core, not your arms.
Pull back with your lats, under control.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Low back arching at the far end.

handlingMistakes.fix: Build up on your knees with a short roll-out.

rows.means: Your abs are holding your body straight.
Your lats pull you back in.
Fault: an arching low back can result in injury.
rows.fix: Roll out less far and slower.

risks.risk: An arching or rotating torso can result in injury.
Rolling out too fast can increase the risk of arching or rotating.
A fall in a standing rollout has caused serious spine injury.

zooms.right: Straight line from knees to head.

libraryDiff.why: core and abs primary, lats secondary fit the sources (c9, c10). StrengthLog also names the obliques; front_delts stays a stabilizer (no source for or against).

loadProgression.text: Lengthen the roll-out step by step; move to the standing version only when experienced.

safetyPoints: Load progression by range and kneeling-to-standing: c7, with the readiness test c6.
Range limiter: rolling toward a wall that stops the wheel (c7).
Bar path clear of the neck: not applicable (no bar).

gaps: Way out (LR-3, LIB-WAYOUT): what to do when you can't roll back (lowering to the floor safely). No source found; no way-out line is shown.
Thumb and wrist on the wheel handles (push archetype, LIB-12 hand pair): no rollout source.
Fault frequency: no source measures how often each rollout fault happens; the top fault follows LR-31 step 2 and step 3's count (plate.mistake.rankNote).
notes: Anchor: StrengthLog's ab-exercises page (sl-abex) has the fullest how-to and muscles; its kneeling-rollout page (sl-abwheel) is short. Both read in full. BarBend has no single ab-wheel page (404); its best-ab-exercises and ab-rollouts pages are used.
c10 is the Power Wheel roll-out (a different wheel device), applied by similarity (MECH); StrengthLog cites the same paper for the ab wheel.
c8 is a two-case report; the shown risk line keeps 'has caused' and does not give a rate. The fall cases were standing rollouts after drinking; no line on alcohol is shown.
The back row restates the sources' own fault and fix (c3, c5, c6, c7), no added cause (LR-6); the back box link stays pending (LR-26, LR-27).
